subject: Biochemistry
vignette: A 44-year-old woman has a 2-year history of chronic diarrhea, 8 kg of weight loss, and a microcytic anemia. Duodenal biopsy shows villous atrophy and intraepithelial lymphocytes consistent with celiac disease. Despite a normal intake of fruits, vegetables, and animal products, she now reports poor vision at night and dry, gritty eyes. Examination reveals conjunctival xerosis with a small foamy plaque adjacent to the limbus.
question: Which of the following best explains the development of her ocular findings?

options.text: Impaired hepatic conversion of retinol to its storage ester
Increased renal clearance of retinol-binding protein
Excessive intake of carotenoids causing pigment deposition
Decreased intestinal absorption of fat-soluble vitamins with the steatorrhea
Reduced synthesis of rhodopsin because of a primary opsin mutation

explanation_correct: Fat-soluble vitamins A, D, E, and K require bile emulsification, pancreatic enzymes, and an intact mucosa for absorption. In untreated celiac disease the resulting steatorrhea produces vitamin A deficiency despite adequate dietary intake, causing night blindness and xerophthalmia with Bitot spots; the other fat-soluble vitamins are characteristically deficient as well.

explanation_incorrect.A: Hepatic esterification and storage of retinol are not the limiting step in this patient; the intestine cannot deliver absorbed vitamin to the liver in the first place.
explanation_incorrect.B: Retinol is transported bound to retinol-binding protein and transthyretin; renal loss of this complex can occur in proteinuric states, but her presentation is malabsorptive.
explanation_incorrect.C: Carotenoid excess produces harmless yellow-orange discoloration of the skin (carotenemia) without xerosis or night blindness.
explanation_incorrect.E: A primary opsin or rhodopsin mutation would cause retinal disease such as retinitis pigmentosa, but it does not explain coexisting conjunctival xerosis in a patient with steatorrhea.

educationalObjective: Steatorrhea from mucosal disease causes fat-soluble vitamin deficiency; vitamin A deficiency in this setting produces night blindness and xerophthalmia despite adequate dietary intake.
